headline: Simulated fly brain becomes crypto day trader, 166,700 virtual neurons on GitHub
summary: An engineer has created an open-source simulation where a fruit fly brain with 166,700 virtual neurons trades crypto, getting dopamine hits for profitable moves.
details: An engineer from Coinbase has developed "Stonkfly," an open-source project that simulates a male fruit fly brain and eyes to act as a crypto day trader. The virtual fly is shown candlestick graphs of historical pricing and can choose to buy, sell, or hold various currencies.

Profitable trades trigger a dopamine rush as a positive reinforcement signal to 15 cells, while losses activate two aversive cells. Notably, the simulated fly cannot use leveraged positions or shorts, demonstrating a cautious approach to trading.

The brain simulation features 166,700 neurons and 25.6 million connections. The virtual fly perceives the graph via a 320x180 display, with its photoreceptor cells receiving RGB pixel values rather than direct pricing data.
The fly "thinks" and acts every 500 milliseconds, with market data refreshing every 60 seconds. It can place up to 24 orders a day, betting a maximum of $10 on each.

The author cautions that the project does not prove actual trading ability and warns against assuming that synapse changes indicate skill, especially given general rises in crypto prices. The simulation primarily illustrates the connection between input mechanisms, visual signals, and neural changes.

To run Stonkfly, users need macOS or Linux, 16 GB of RAM, Python 3.11, and a C++ 17 compiler. The simulation defaults to paper trades with a $100 virtual balance using real BTC-to-USDC data, and instructions are provided for setting up a live trading account.

headline_marked: [[AI multi-agent framework stole thousands of credentials]] in under six hours
headline: AI multi-agent framework stole thousands of credentials in under six hours
summary: Google's Threat Intelligence Group reports an autonomous multi-agent system compromised cloud infrastructure and harvested thousands of credentials in less than six hours, operating with minimal human intervention.
details: Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) documented a mass credential-harvesting campaign in Q3 2026. A financially motivated actor deployed an autonomous multi-agent system within an organization's cloud infrastructure, allowing requests to originate from legitimate-looking IP addresses.

The attacker reportedly built this framework using an AI coding chatbot, a set of instructions, and preconfigured Markdown files as operational playbooks. This design mirrors the "agent skills" pattern legitimate teams use to give LLMs structured, reusable procedures.

According to Mandiant's analysis cited in GTIG's report, the system autonomously managed vulnerability scanning, collected credentials, resolved technical problems, and rotated IP addresses. The entire operation, from setup to compromising thousands of third-party credentials, took under six hours.

This incident highlights a significant security risk: the same reliability engineering that makes agents useful—self-correction, retries, and graceful handling of failures—also makes offensive attack pipelines resilient and capable of running unattended for extended periods.

The core point is that the barrier to executing sophisticated, multi-day human-operated campaigns has dropped. It now requires only the ability to write effective agent instructions, rather than needing advanced, dangerous AI capabilities beyond what a decent coding agent already possesses.

For organizations utilizing agentic coding tools, CI-integrated assistants, or internal automation with cloud credentials, this campaign offers a preview of what a compromise of such infrastructure looks like from an attacker's perspective.

GTIG's report describes the campaign's structure and outcome but does not name the specific AI coding chatbot used or publish the full Markdown playbooks. This makes it a capability disclosure rather than an immediate incident-response playbook, with more operational detail expected to emerge.
